content.title: About
content.content: Almonds are the edible seeds of the almond tree (Prunus dulcis), which is native to the Middle East and Central Asia and is now grown in many warm regions of the world. They have a mild, slightly sweet, nutty flavor and a crunchy texture. Almonds are eaten raw, roasted, or blanched and are used in baking, desserts, spreads, and almond milk.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Almonds are related to peaches, plums, and cherries, and the almond itself is the seed inside the fruit's pit.
Sweet almonds are the ones eaten as food; bitter almonds contain compounds that are toxic when raw and are not sold as ordinary snacks.
Almond trees have been cultivated for thousands of years.
Almonds are used to make almond flour, almond butter, marzipan, and almond milk.
Almond blossoms appear in early spring, before the leaves.

items.title: Rich in vitamin E
items.content: Almonds are one of the best food sources of vitamin E, an antioxidant that helps protect cells.

items.title: Provides healthy fats
items.content: Almonds contain mostly monounsaturated fats, which can be part of a heart-friendly diet.

items.title: Contains magnesium
items.content: Magnesium supports normal muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Provides protein and fiber
items.content: Almonds contribute plant protein and fiber, which support fullness.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Almonds contain more calcium than most other nuts.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: Almonds can cause allergic reactions, which may be severe in some people.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Almonds are calorie-dense, so portions should be moderate.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: Whole almonds are not suitable for young children because they can cause choking.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Almonds contain oxalates, which people prone to kidney stones may need to limit. Bitter almonds should never be eaten raw.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Almonds can be eaten as a snack, added to oatmeal, yogurt, salads, and baked goods, or ground into almond flour and almond butter. Soaking or blanching almonds softens them and makes the skins easy to remove. Unsalted or lightly salted almonds are a good option.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store almonds in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer storage, keep them in the refrigerator or freezer, since their oils can turn rancid. Discard almonds that smell bitter, sharp, or stale.

content.title: About
content.content: Cashews are the edible seeds of the cashew tree (Anacardium occidentale), native to tropical regions. Salt adds a mildly salty flavor and a crunchy texture. Cashews are eaten raw, roasted, and used in cooking for sauces, desserts, and baked goods.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The cashew fruit forms a "pseudo‑fruit" called the cashew apple, with the nut hanging below it.
Cashews are rich in iron, magnesium, and copper, making them a valuable mineral source.
African and South American countries are the main producers of cashews.
Cashews are often processed into cashew oil, butter (cashew paste), and vegan cheese alternatives.
The salt used on salted cashews is typically sea or Himalayan salt to enhance the nut's natural flavor.

items.title: Rich in healthy fats
items.content: Cashews contain monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids that support heart health.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: A 100‑g serving provides about 18 g of plant protein, helping maintain muscle mass.

items.title: Contains magnesium and copper
items.content: These minerals are involved in energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Supports bone health
items.content: Cashews provide phosphorus and calcium, contributing to bone strength.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: They contain tocopherols and phenolic compounds that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: Cashews can trigger severe allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Due to their fat content, cashews are calorie‑dense, so portion control is advised.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Salted cashews contain added sodium, which may be a concern for people with hypertension.

items.title: Raw toxicity
items.content: Raw cashews contain urushiol, a toxic compound, so they are always heat‑treated before sale.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Salted cashews make a convenient snack, can be added to salads, rice or noodle dishes, and used in sauces and spreads. Lightly roasting them enhances their aroma.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cashews in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent fat oxidation.

double-cheeseburger-on-wheat-bun-2-small.title: Double Cheeseburger on Wheat Bun, 2 Small Patties

content.title: About
content.content: The double cheeseburger consists of a wheat bun, two small beef patties, melted cheese, lettuce, tomato, pickles, onion and sauce. It offers a balanced mix of tender meat, gooey cheese and fresh vegetables.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: A wheat bun gives a softer texture compared with a classic white bun.
Two small patties allow better portion control and protein distribution.
The combination of processed cheese and beef creates the characteristic creamy flavor popular in fast‑food.
The original recipe uses a mayo‑mustard based sauce that enhances the overall aroma.

items.title: Protein
items.content: Beef patties provide a high‑quality source of complete protein essential for muscle repair.

items.title: Calcium
items.content: Melted cheese contributes calcium, supporting bone and dental health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat is rich in B12 and B6 vitamins, important for nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Dietary Fiber
items.content: Lettuce, tomato and pickles add a modest amount of fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: Energy Supply
items.content: Carbohydrates from the bun and fats from the cheese provide a quick source of energy.

items.title: High Caloric Content
items.content: The combination of meat, cheese and bun makes the burger calorie‑dense; portion control is advised for weight‑watchers.

items.title: Saturated Fats
items.content: Processed cheese and beef contain saturated fats, which can affect cholesterol levels if consumed in excess.

items.title: Dairy Allergy
items.content: Cheese may trigger allergic reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Sauces and pickles can add significant sodium, which should be limited by people with hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the burger hot, split the bun, place the cheese‑topped patties, add vegetables and sauce. It is convenient to eat with hands, though a knife and fork can be used if preferred.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the assembled burger in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. For longer storage, separate the components: patties and bun can be frozen for up to 2 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Fruit and vegetable smoothie, bottled is a ready‑to‑drink beverage made from a blend of fresh fruits and vegetables, sometimes combined with water, juice, or plant‑based milks. The product is pasteurized and sealed in a hermetic bottle, providing a long shelf life without refrigeration until opened.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Blends can contain more than 10 different fruits and vegetables, delivering a broad spectrum of vitamins and minerals.
Bottles are often made from PET, which is fully recyclable.
Pasteurization retains most vitamin C, though some heat‑sensitive compounds may be partially degraded.
Many smoothies are fortified with probiotics or plant proteins to boost nutritional value.
Flavor and color depend on fruit‑to‑vegetable ratios; adding carrot or beet gives a vivid hue.

items.title: Rich in vitamins and antioxidants
items.content: The fruit‑vegetable blend provides vitamin C, vitamin A (beta‑carotene), vitamin K, folate, and polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Dietary fiber from the fruits and vegetables promotes regular bowel movements and a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: High water content contributes to overall fluid balance.

items.title: Low added sugar (when formulated responsibly)
items.content: Some brands keep added sugars minimal, making the drink suitable for blood‑glucose management.

items.title: Convenient and portable
items.content: A ready‑to‑drink format makes it easy to increase daily fruit and vegetable intake on the go.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Certain products add significant amounts of sugar or fruit syrups, which can raise calorie count.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Formulations may contain nuts, soy, or dairy ingredients; always check the label.

items.title: Loss of some nutrients
items.content: Heat from pasteurization can reduce levels of heat‑sensitive vitamins such as vitamin C.

items.title: Preservatives and additives
items.content: To extend shelf life, some brands use preservatives that may be undesirable for sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Store the bottle in a cool, dry place; after opening, keep it refrigerated and consume within 3‑5 days. Drink chilled or at room temperature, optionally over ice. Shake gently before drinking to mix any settled pulp.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the unopened bottle away from direct sunlight in a cool, dry environment. Once opened, refrigerate and finish within the indicated period. Discard the product after the expiration date printed on the label.

content.title: About
content.content: Lima beans are large, buttery legumes also known as butter beans. In this product they are flash‑frozen right after harvest and contain no added fat. The beans have a tender, slightly sweet flesh and retain most of their nutrients thanks to rapid freezing.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lima beans originate from South America, especially Peru and Bolivia.
They are among the largest edible beans, reaching up to 10 cm in length.
Freezing preserves their bright green color and delicate flavor better than canning.
Beans are rich in plant protein and complex carbohydrates, providing sustained energy.
Botanically they belong to the Fabaceae family and can fix nitrogen in the soil.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: One cup of cooked lima beans provides about 15 g of protein, supporting tissue growth and repair.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood glucose levels.

items.title: Contains potassium and magnesium
items.content: These minerals support heart, muscle, and nervous system function.

items.title: Source of folate (vitamin B9)
items.content: Folate is essential for DNA synthesis and is especially important for pregnant women.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The absence of added fat makes these beans suitable for low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans, including lima beans.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce mineral absorption; soaking or cooking helps mitigate this.

items.title: Gas formation
items.content: Beans can cause increased gas in sensitive people; gradual introduction to the diet can help.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Frozen lima beans are easy to steam, boil, or add to soups. They work well in salads, stews, pasta dishes, and vegetable casseroles. For cooking, quickly thaw in the microwave or under running water.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the package in a freezer at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. Once thawed, use within 2–3 days and do not refreeze.

content.title: About
content.content: The oatmeal snack bar is a ready‑to‑eat portable snack made from whole oat flakes, dried fruit, nuts and sometimes sweeteners like honey or chocolate. It has a soft yet chewy texture, a mildly sweet flavor, and provides lasting satiety.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Oat flakes are a source of beta‑glucan, a soluble fiber that helps regulate blood sugar.
Many snack bars are made using a no‑bake process, preserving more of the oats' nutrients.
Recipes often include “super‑foods” such as chia seeds, hemp hearts or goji berries.
Oat bars are convenient to carry: they don’t crumble and don’t require refrigeration.
In some countries oatmeal bars are marketed as an “energy” product for athletes.

items.title: Rich in beta‑glucan
items.content: Beta‑glucan can help lower cholesterol and support immune function.

items.title: Contains complex carbohydrates
items.content: Oats release glucose slowly, providing steady energy for several hours.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: Oats and added nuts/seeds provide about 5–7 g of protein per serving.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B2 and B6 are involved in energy metabolism.

items.title: Nut/gluten allergy
items.content: Bars may contain nuts, seeds and oats, which have gluten, important for people with allergies or celiac disease.

items.title: Added sugars
items.content: Some bars are sweetened with honey, agave syrup or sugar, increasing their calorie load.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: One bar typically provides 180–250 kcal; portion control is advised for weight‑loss plans.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The bar can be eaten straight from the wrapper as a snack between meals, chopped into yogurt or kefir, or broken into pieces to add crunch to granola or salads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store bars in a cool, dry place, in their original packaging or an airtight container. For longer storage (over 3 months) keep them in the refrigerator to prevent drying out and spoilage.

content.title: About
content.content: The “Chocolate Cola” soft drink combines the classic cola taste with notes of milk chocolate. It contains water, sugar, caramel color, flavorings, caffeine and natural chocolate extract. The result is a sweet, slightly bitter aftertaste with characteristic fizz.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first chocolate‑flavored cola appeared in the early 2000s as a limited edition.
The cola‑chocolate combo is especially popular in Japan, where such flavors are common in vending machines.
A hint of vanilla is often added to soften the overall flavor profile.
Caffeine content is usually about 30 mg per 100 ml, comparable to regular cola.
The drink is frequently used in cocktail mixes, such as the “Chocolate Fizz.”

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Sugar and caffeine provide a quick rise in energy, useful for moments requiring heightened alertness.

items.title: Mood enhancement
items.content: Chocolate aroma stimulates serotonin production, helping improve mood.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Like any soft drink, it contributes to overall fluid intake.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Regular consumption can lead to weight gain and increase the risk of dental caries.

items.title: Caffeine
items.content: Caffeine‑sensitive individuals may experience insomnia, rapid heartbeat, or anxiety.

items.title: Carbonation
items.content: Carbonated drinks can cause heartburn or stomach discomfort in some people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve chilled, straight from the bottle or a glass. Pairs well with ice cream, desserts, and works as a base for mixed drinks.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep the cap tightly sealed to preserve carbonation.
